objective.n: Several weather words fit some blanks; the most natural choice is given first.

s: i. Same shade of meaning: big – large – enormous; shout – yell – bellow; nibble – eat – gobble; scared – frightened – terrified; toss – throw – slam; misting – sprinkling – pouring.
ii. Stronger word: 1. screamed; 2. freezing; 3. furious; 4. pouring; 5. gigantic.
iii. Weaker word: 1. whispered; 2. cool; 3. cross; 4. sprinkling; 5. big.

shortQuestions: The theme is the comparison between a father's love for his child and God's mercy for mankind. Just as the father forgives his son after seeing his childish toys, God will forgive human beings who, like children, are busy with worldly 'toys' and fail to understand His commands.

The poet's little son disobeyed him for the seventh time, so the poet struck him and sent him to bed without a kiss. Later, feeling sorry, he went to the child's room and found him asleep with tear-stained eyes. Beside the bed the boy had placed his little toys — a box of counters, a red-veined stone, a piece of glass, shells, bluebells and coins — to comfort himself. The father wept and prayed that God would be merciful to people as he had now felt for his son.
The poem is written in irregular (free) verse — an ode-like style with lines of varying length and an irregular rhyme scheme, close to the rhythm of natural speech.

Yes. The irregular lines and natural speech rhythm suit the personal, emotional and confessional mood; they express the father's changing feelings — anger, regret, tenderness and prayer — sincerely and naturally.

The toys symbolise the worldly things that human beings value and play with — wealth, power and pleasures — which are as trivial in God's sight as the child's toys are to an adult. They also show the child's innocence and the comfort we seek in small things.

The poet compares himself to God: as he, a father, forgave his son after seeing his innocence and sorrow, he hopes that God, who is far more fatherly and merciful than he, will forgive human beings for their childish behaviour and sins on the Day of Judgement.

The tone is sad, regretful and tender, ending in a prayerful, hopeful note. Yes, it matches the theme: the regret of the father leads to his realisation of God's mercy, so the gentle, sorrowful tone fits the message of love and forgiveness.

The poem evokes feelings of sympathy for the innocent child, regret for harsh treatment, tenderness and love between parent and child, and hope and gratitude for the infinite mercy of Allah. It teaches us to be gentle and forgiving.
activities: Paraphrase: Then (on the Day of Judgement), O God, You — who are no less fatherly than I, Your creature whom You have made from clay — will give up Your anger and say, "I will forgive them for their childish behaviour." The poet hopes that God, like a loving father, will pity and forgive human beings for their foolishness just as he forgave his son.

Oral recount guide: students share a real experience — e.g., "Once my father scolded me for breaking a glass. I cried and went to my room. Later he came, sat beside me and explained gently. I felt loved and learned to be careful." They should describe what happened, how they felt and what they learned.
